articles.body:
China

At a neon-lit electronics market in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, buyers from Africa to Bangladesh are snapping up dozens of used smartphones.

The number is mind-boggling. As the world's largest smartphone producer, China discards over 400 million devices annually.

"From all China, the broken mobile phones come here," said Pakistani businessman Akhtar Muhammad as he browsed the stacks of devices.

"We will buy the new LCDs, send the broken phones to our countries, also buy LCDs from here take them to Pakistan where we will fix them," he said.

Chip shortages and rising prices are making new devices harder to afford and in emerging markets in Africa and South Asia the demand for used models is soaring.

Counterpoint Research says the global secondary smartphone market grew 13 per cent year-on-year in the first half of 2026 to 150 million units.

Mama, a young Nigerian buyer, said he had bought around 40 used phones in one day in Shenzhen.

"They are more expensive in Africa because we don't have big suppliers or markets like this one," he said. "If I buy and send them to my country, I get profit."

But near the market in Shenzhen, a new and more formalised alternative is taking root. PaiJiTang Mall is a self-service second-hand marketplace run by Chinese recycling company ATRenew.

Inside, rows of over 20,000 used phones are on display. Buyers scan QR codes for instant inspection reports and pricing, test the units and purchase in bulk.

The shop draws up to 1,000 visitors daily, with international traders making up about a third, said store manager Zhang Xiaoming.

Algerian shopkeeper, Abdul Rahim, says he flies to China up to three times a month to stock his phone and accessory store, capitalising on a price gap of $110 to $132 per device.

"It's very easy for Algerians to get the visa to China. You put in your papers and in two or three days you have the visa in your passport," he said.

At ATRenew's massive processing hub in Dongguan, north of Shenzhen, roughly 30,000 second-hand gadgets arrive daily and are inspected and packed by over 300 technicians.

Its quality control manager, Li Cankang, says its daily outbound shipments are at a similar level.

Apple devices account for 70 to 80 per cent of sales, with the rest split among Chinese brands.

Counterpoint says while older models like the iPhone 11, 12, and 13 are losing ground to cheap Androids in China, they retain strong brand power overseas, where they find a second life.

articles.body:
In public, Andy Burnham’s recent focus has been on securing better trade terms with the European Union and reforming Britain’s welfare system. In private, the prime minister has been preoccupied by a more global problem: what happens next in the Iran war.

For several weeks, Burnham and his most senior Cabinet colleagues have been consumed by the possibility Donald Trump could resume major strikes on Iran, according to people familiar with the matter. While the U.K. has taken hope the Republicans’ defeat in the midterms might temper Trump’s foreign policy, ministers see the U.S. president weighing options for a fresh attack, they said, a prospect that appears to have grown in recent days.

Burnham on Friday sealed a deal for closer EU ties that he said could boost the economy by 0.5% a year, bring down food prices and raise the prospect of lower electricity prices. But looming in the background is Iran. Even if Trump decides against resuming his war, the grim reality for Burnham is his officials have told him all plausible outcomes will have a negative impact on the U.K.’s economy and security.

articles.summary: Earlier this week, Trump greeted Putin ahead of a meeting in China and said the pair have a "great relationship".

Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer". articles.body:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.

Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".

Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".

Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials said.

Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.

On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.

The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.

Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".

"They [Zelensky and Putin] both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.

Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.

However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".

"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he told CNN.

Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he was a "friend" meant "he doesn't feel enough pressure".

The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the south-east of the country early on Friday.

Polish Defence Minister WÅadysÅaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

This was about 100km from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the coalition of the willing - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said. Another cruise missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.

On Saturday, Polish Foreign Minister RadosÅaw Sikorski told the BBC the cruise missiles had guidance systems, so "it is very unlikely that they veered off course as a result of Ukrainian electronic warfare".

"This is a war in Europe that affects our security," he told Radio 4's Today programme, also referencing similar incidents in recent months across Europe.

Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said the military alliance had scrambled its jets in response.

Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine.

Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

This comes amid efforts by Indonesia to strengthen enforcement, bolster market integrity and protect investors.

JAKARTA: Indonesia's Financial Services Authority (OJK) on Saturday (Nov 21) announced sanctions in 10 capital market violation cases, amid efforts to strengthen enforcement, bolster market integrity and protect investors.

OJK ordered the return of 23.77 billion rupiah (US$1.3 million) in illicit gains from three stock manipulation cases, involving shares of PT Grand House Mulia, PT Saraswanti Anugerah Makmur and PT Suryamas Dutamakmur.

In the Grand House Mulia case, OJK also ordered the closure of 15 securities accounts linked to the trading activity between March and July 2023.

The agency also imposed a total of 3.71 billion rupiah in administrative fines on seven listed companies for disclosure failures, material and affiliated-party transaction breaches, financial reporting violations and non-compliance with share transfer obligations.

OJK also barred multiple individuals involved in the manipulation cases from participating in Indonesia's capital markets, derivatives and carbon exchange sectors for periods ranging from three to 10 years.

OJK previously sanctioned three listed firms as part of Indonesia's market reforms following concerns raised by global index providers over the transparency and investability of Indonesia's capital markets.

articles.title: Meta's India offices hit by opposition protests over account removals
articles.summary: Debate is growing in India about potential risks to free speech from the increasingly strict efforts of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government to remove social media content it objects to.
articles.preview: Debate is growing in India about potential risks to free speech from the increasingly strict efforts of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government to remove social media content it objects to. NEW DELHI: The youth wing of India's main opposition Congress party clashed with police outside Meta offices, protesting the company's removal of some Instagram accounts of its members, according to footage released by the group on Saturday (Nov 21).
articles.body:
Debate is growing in India about potential risks to free speech from the increasingly strict efforts of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government to remove social media content it objects to.

NEW DELHI: The youth wing of India's main opposition Congress party clashed with police outside Meta offices, protesting the company's removal of some Instagram accounts of its members, according to footage released by the group on Saturday (Nov 21).

Meta declined to comment on the protests, an escalation by the influential political group in the company's biggest market by users. Debate is growing in India about potential risks to free speech from the increasingly strict efforts of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government to remove social media content it objects to.

Modi's government says it orders content taken down only if it breaches local laws, can harm public safety or national security. Congress has long accused Meta and other social media platforms of curbing dissent online by removing party accounts, favouring Modi's government.

Meta has said it restricts content in India to comply with local laws.

MODI'S PARTY ACCUSES CONGRESS OF VANDALISM

Pradeep Bhandari, a national spokesperson for Modi's ruling party, criticised Congress' actions on Saturday, saying they had "not only vandalised and destroyed Meta's office in Hyderabad" but were also "flaunting it on social media".

"This is Congress Model: Vandalise offices of Private companies," he wrote.

India's IT ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

In Hyderabad on Friday, protesters carrying placards chanted slogans as they stormed into the building that houses Meta's offices, smashing plants to the ground and clashing with police, according to footage released by the Indian Youth Congress' X account.

Another video showed Congress workers spray-painting anti-Meta slogans on walls outside the building that houses its Mumbai office, clashing with security guards who tried to stop them.

In Gurugram near New Delhi, Congress workers chanted slogans and held banners reading "restore youth Congress accounts", official online posts showed.

The Indian Youth Congress posted warnings on X that it would "storm your offices across the country and stage protests" unless Instagram accounts of its leaders are restored.

Two such accounts were restored after Friday's protests, but thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted, Manu Jain, who is in charge of social media for the youth group, told Reuters on Saturday.

Meta must explain how its algorithms restrict posts and must restore accounts taken down on government orders, he added.

Reporters Without Borders has said the removal of journalistic content from social media has been on the rise in India this year, and free-speech activists say a new government rule gives social media companies hardly any time to review and decide on takedown requests.

In February, Modi's government ordered social media companies to take down unlawful content within three hours of being notified about it, tightening an earlier 36-hour timeline.

Meta disclosures show that it restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India under local laws in the first half of 2026, second only to Indonesia and up from about 70,000 in the preceding six months.

"The large majority of these items included instances where we were obligated to proactively restrict content ... based on local law requirements," Meta said.

articles.body:
L'Fbi sta indagando su una presunta violazione del suo database nazionale di informazioni criminali, uno strumento fondamentale che funge da collegamento tra le forze dell'ordine federali, statali e locali; la notizia è stata riferita alla Cnn da due persone informate sull'indagine.

L'intrusione nel National Crime Information Center (Ncic) da parte di presunti hacker rappresenta il secondo episodio di questo tipo negli ultimi mesi.

A settembre, un gruppo noto come "ShinyHunters" ha preso di mira i dati personali sensibili dei dipendenti, sottraendoli da un portale dell'Fbi dedicato alle offerte di lavoro.

La scoperta di questa recente intrusione, scrive ancora la Cnn, avviene in un momento in cui l'amministrazione Trump sta cercando di placare le preoccupazioni dell'opinione pubblica riguardo alla sicurezza informatica nazionale, a seguito di una serie di interruzioni di alto profilo che hanno colpito banche, la National Security Agency (Nsa) e il sistema di controllo del traffico aereo della Faa. L'Fbi non ha risposto immediatamente a una richiesta di commento.

Giovedì, dopo che i funzionari dell'agenzia sono venuti a conoscenza dell'ultimo incidente informatico, il direttore dell'Fbi Kash Patel è intervenuto su Fox News per illustrare l'impegno dell'FBI nel campo della sicurezza informatica.

Patel ha colto l'occasione per parlare di un'operazione, conclusasi mesi fa, volta a sollecitare le aziende ad aggiornare i propri sistemi per impedire agli hacker di accedere a dati sensibili.

Patel ha fatto riferimento all'operazione 'Winter Shield' come se fosse ancora in corso, lodando l'attuale amministrazione per aver provveduto ad aggiornare sistemi chiave destinati a proteggere le infrastrutture critiche del Paese. "Altre amministrazioni avrebbero potuto effettuare questi aggiornamenti, ma non lo hanno fatto", ha dichiarato. "Noi stiamo giocando d'anticipo e recuperando il tempo perduto".

articles.title: Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as Iran tightens grip on shipping
articles.summary: British maritime agency reports two incidents near Oman, while Iran says a tanker caught fire due to naval mine.
articles.preview: British maritime agency reports two incidents near Oman, while Iran says a tanker caught fire due to naval mine. British maritime authorities have reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran continues to restrict shipping through the vital waterway. The incidents were reported on Saturday near Oman, amid a war involving Tehran, Washington and Tel Aviv that began with the United States and Israel attacking Iran in late February.
articles.body:
British maritime agency reports two incidents near Oman, while Iran says a tanker caught fire due to naval mine.

British maritime authorities have reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran continues to restrict shipping through the vital waterway.

The incidents were reported on Saturday near Oman, amid a war involving Tehran, Washington and Tel Aviv that began with the United States and Israel attacking Iran in late February.

Tehran has since sought to tighten its control over the strait, which carried nearly a fifth of the world’s crude oil supplies before the conflict.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre, a British agency that monitors threats to commercial shipping, said one tanker was hit at its rear about 20km (13 miles) north of Khasab, a port town on Oman’s northern coast.

Another tanker was struck in its engine room about 31km (20 miles) east of Khasab, the agency said.

No casualties were reported, but it remained unclear whether the two incidents involved separate vessels.

Iran’s navy said on Saturday that an oil tanker had caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait.

In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the navy accused the vessel of ignoring warnings and travelling with its identification and navigation equipment switched off.

The Iranian account could not be independently verified, and it was unclear whether the burning tanker was involved in either incident reported by UKMTO.

A ‘pattern’

Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week.

Citing statements issued by Iran’s armed forces, Serdar said about 25 incidents had been reported since the previous Saturday, averaging roughly three a day, a trend he called “quite dramatic”.

“This is becoming a pattern,” Serdar said, explaining that “Iranians are saying the Strait of Hormuz is under their control; that any ship that is passing through the Strait of Hormuz has to be in full coordination with the Iranian authorities and must follow the roads and the lanes that are determined by Iran.”

If ships do not comply, Iran says “they are either going to be attacked, or they are going to hit the sea mines that are laid by the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC or the Iranian forces”, Serdar added.

Our correspondent said Tehran was deliberately escalating tensions to send a message that if Iran could not export its oil, other countries would not be able to do so either.

He said Iran was also seeking to show that it remained in control of the strait, a narrow passage connecting the Gulf with international shipping routes.

The US has responded to Iran’s restrictions by blockading Iranian ports and deploying naval vessels to escort tankers through the waterway.

The confrontation has raised concerns over the security of a major route for global energy supplies, with commercial vessels caught in the struggle between Washington and Tehran over access to the strait.

articles.title: Russia strikes Zelenskyy's hometown, killing 2
articles.summary: The attacks follow Russian President Vladimir Putin's vow of a "painful" response to Ukraine's attacks this week on the Kerch Bridge, linking Russian-occupied Crimea.
articles.preview: November 21, 2026 The attacks follow Russian President Vladimir Putin's vow of a "painful" response to Ukraine's attacks this week on the Kerch Bridge, linking Russian-occupied Crimea. Russian ballistic missile strikes on Ukraine's southern city of Kryvyi Rih — President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown — killed two people and wounded dozens of others, local officials said Saturday.
articles.body:
November 21, 2026

The attacks follow Russian President Vladimir Putin's vow of a "painful" response to Ukraine's attacks this week on the Kerch Bridge, linking Russian-occupied Crimea.

Russian ballistic missile strikes on Ukraine's southern city of Kryvyi Rih — President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown — killed two people and wounded dozens of others, local officials said Saturday.

The attacks come amid little progress in talks to end the nearly five-year-old war and after Ukraine, on three occasions this week, struck the Kerch bridge linking Russian-occupied Crimea with Russia.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had vowed a "painful" response to the Kerch attack, as the bridge is vital for war supplies for Russian forces in the south.

What do we know?

Among the dead in Friday evening's double-tap strikes on Kryvyi Rih were a 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman, while several children were among the 60 wounded, the Ukrainian officials said.

Several fires broke out and damage was caused to about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and an industrial facility, Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration, wrote on Telegram.

Moscow, meanwhile, confirmed a further strike on Friday night in Kryvyi Rih.

Russia's Defense Ministry said a thermal power plant in the city was hit, along with a power substation in the region of Rivne, on the opposite side of the country.

Both facilities supply electricity to the industry supporting Ukraine's military, the ministry added.

What are the other latest developments?

Elsewhere in the nearly five-year-long war, Russia also struck a cargo vessel near Odesa, which Moscow said was carrying dual-use goods for the Ukrainian military.

Eleven people, including two children, were wounded when a Russian drone attacked a five-story apartment building in the northeastern Kharkiv region, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said Saturday.

One person was wounded in a Russian attack on the capital, Kyiv, according to the service.

In Russia, local officials said Saturday that Ukrainian drone attacks wounded three people in the Bryansk and Belgorod border regions.

Finland, meanwhile, said it detected a drone attack on Saturday morning on a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea, prompting Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to warn that the war is "spilling over into our immediate vicinity."

After damage to Russia's Kerch bridge to Crimea, Zelenskyy warned in an interview with US broadcaster NBC that the structure "will not remain standing anyway."

articles.title: Could Iran reverse its stated policy of a civil-only nuclear programme?
articles.summary: Iran's FM Araghchi says there is 'major strategic debate' about the future of Iran's nuclear doctrine.
articles.preview: Iran’s FM Araghchi says there is ‘major strategic debate’ about the future of Iran’s nuclear doctrine. Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said the country’s stockpile of enriched uranium will be used according to its needs, “however they are defined”, as he spoke about possible changes to Iran’s longstanding nuclear doctrine. Araghchi’s comments during an interview with Iranian media on Saturday have increased speculation that Iran may be moving away from its policy of limiting its nuclear programme to civilian purposes amid its conflict with…
articles.body:
Iran’s FM Araghchi says there is ‘major strategic debate’ about the future of Iran’s nuclear doctrine.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said the country’s stockpile of enriched uranium will be used according to its needs, “however they are defined”, as he spoke about possible changes to Iran’s longstanding nuclear doctrine.

Araghchi’s comments during an interview with Iranian media on Saturday have increased speculation that Iran may be moving away from its policy of limiting its nuclear programme to civilian purposes amid its conflict with the United States.

The future of Iran’s nuclear programme has become a major sticking point in efforts to end the war, with Washington insisting that it must have guarantees that Iran will never develop a nuclear weapon before it will agree to a full ceasefire.

So, is Iran’s nuclear policy changing, and what could that mean for the conflict?

What is Iran’s official nuclear policy?

Iran has consistently maintained that its nuclear programme is for peaceful purposes only, such as for electricity generation, medical research and agriculture.

This policy has been underlined by a decades-old religious decree, or fatwa, issued by the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, banning the development of nuclear weapons.

However, Iran has also insisted it has the right to enrich uranium for these purposes under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), which it joined in 1970. It has called this right “non-negotiable”.

What have Araghchi and other officials said?

In an interview with Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency on Saturday, Araghchi reiterated that Iran’s stockpile of enriched material would remain inside the country.

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) estimated in 2025 – before Israel launched strikes on Iran in June that year – that Iran had about 440 kilogrammes (970 pounds) of uranium enriched to about 60 percent. This is short of the 90 percent required for making nuclear weapons, but is the level at which it becomes much quicker to reach 90 percent. It is also far beyond the roughly 3 percent needed for power generation.

This material, Araghchi said during his interview, would “be used according to our needs however those needs are defined”.

Araghchi also made reference to an ongoing debate among lawmakers and officials in Iran about altering its nuclear doctrine, and said people on both sides of that debate have “strong arguments”.

“This is a major strategic debate, and there is nothing wrong with examining it seriously because it directly concerns national interests and security,” Araghchi said, adding that those in favour of reform argue Iran’s current approach of no nuclear weapons has “failed to protect” the country’s nuclear facilities, which have come under attack from US and Israeli forces both last year and this year.

However, Araghchi acknowledged that any official change to the policy would have “far-reaching consequences”.

“For now, our doctrine has not changed, and our official position remains the same,” he said.

Other Iranian officials have also spoken about a potential review of the country’s nuclear doctrine. Earlier this month, security chief Mohsen Rezaei said “there is a discussion on whether we want to continue to follow the previous nuclear doctrine in the event of a new war breaking out”, though he also stressed that Tehran has not yet made any change.

On November 12, Iran’s Assembly of Experts, the body that appoints the supreme leader, said reviewing “the country’s defence doctrine and establishing the necessary deterrence have become unavoidable necessities”.

Ali Fathollah-Nejad, a German-Iranian political scientist who directs the Center for Middle East and Global Order (CMEG), told Al Jazeera the move by the Assembly of Experts “appears to mark the first time a governing institution has endorsed this position”.

Why do the US and Israel think Iran is developing nuclear weapons?

Besides being a signatory to the NPT in 1970, Iran also initially complied with a nuclear agreement it struck with the US and other global powers in 2015 – the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), which required it to limit uranium enrichment to very low levels and undergo inspections.

But after Washington pulled out of the deal in 2018 under the first administration of US President Donald Trump, Tehran eventually went back to intensifying its nuclear programme and abandoned restrictions imposed by the deal.

In June 2025, the IAEA’s board of governors declared Iran was no longer complying with its commitment to international nuclear safeguards. Tehran rejected that report and accused the IAEA of giving a pretext for US and Israeli attacks targeting Iranian nuclear facilities, including Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan, just days later during the 12-day war.

In March of this year, IAEA chief Rafael Grossi said at least 200kg (440lbs) of Iran’s enriched material was believed to have survived the US-Israeli attacks and was likely buried underground in or near the Isfahan nuclear facility site.

Grossi has since said the agency cannot verify the amount or location of Iran’s enriched material due to a lack of access.

The IAEA has called Iran’s enrichment level “a matter of serious concern”, while the US has pointed to it as evidence that Iran is pursuing nuclear weapons despite its official policy.

“If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60 percent enriched fuel?” US Vice President JD Vance said in an interview with the Reuters news agency last month. “And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue.”

President Trump has repeatedly stated that Iran must never be allowed to develop a nuclear weapon.

Officials in Israel, which is widely believed to have its own undeclared nuclear weapons, have also long accused Iran of pursuing nuclear weapons.

“The Iranian regime, which seeks to destroy Israel, is once again working to revive its nuclear programme,” said Israel’s now-caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in an address last week. “We must remove this existential threat once and for all.”

Will Iran officially reverse its no-nuclear-weapons policy?

That remains to be seen, but it is “within the realm of possibility”, Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst and affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies, told Al Jazeera.

He said the US-Israeli war launched against Iran in February this year “has significantly changed all the calculations in Tehran”, with more open discussion about whether to renew the late ayatollah’s ban on nuclear weapons now taking place.

“What used to be a fringe opinion, leaving the NPT and potentially going for a nuclear weapon, is now something that’s within the realm of possibility – even though all the major players are still warning against it,” said Parsi. “It’s not a decision but an indication that deterrence is being rethought in light of the war.”

Simon Mabon, a professor of international politics at Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera that a “broadly rational defensive reason” for potentially shifting Iran’s nuclear policy is emerging within the country, though adding that such a shift would be legally and ethically problematic.

“If you look at the sort of traditional nuclear logic, it says that nuclear weapons play a very strong defensive role in deterring the actions of another state,” Mabon told Al Jazeera. “That would be very sound logic for the Iranians in light of what’s happened.”

“This, of course, is something that’s deeply problematic,” said Mabon. “It goes against the terms of the NPT, it goes against the spirit of the NPT, so it would necessitate withdrawal from that.”

CMEG director Fathollah-Nejad said that there are serious divisions within Iran’s government over the direction of its nuclear programme.

Hardline lawmakers and religious leaders view Iran’s nuclear and missile assets as “indispensable” to “regime security and deterrence”, while a separate camp that includes former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif argues against the development of nuclear arms, saying it would “almost inevitably” trigger further attacks by the US and Israel, said Fathollah-Nejad.

For now, he added, Iran “plays with the ambiguity” of its nuclear policy.

What does this mean for US-Iran negotiations?

Fathollah-Nejad said a shift in Iran’s nuclear doctrine would directly counter the US’s “single most important goal” in the conflict: to secure nuclear concessions from Tehran.

The US has insisted Iran must make nuclear commitments at the outset of any negotiations, while Iran wants its own seven stated conditions met, including lifting the blockade, restoring access to its frozen assets and ending hostilities on all fronts, before even beginning discussions about its nuclear programme.

Mabon said a change in Iran’s nuclear policy “would have a dramatic impact on how the Americans and the Israelis read the next phase of this conflict”, with the Israelis likely believing it necessitates a “return to violence”.

“That’s where some of the other dangers start to come in,” Mabon added. “The shift in Iran’s doctrine, even if it’s meant intentionally as a defensive shift, can easily be read in offensive terms.”

“I think it’s a very, very dangerous moment,” he said.

articles.title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
articles.summary: Ukraine's president says Kyiv acted after 109 separate Russian aerial attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
articles.preview: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine. In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".

He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.

"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.

The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.

"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."

The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.

This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.

Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.

A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.

Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.

"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.

He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".

The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".

Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".

Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".

Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".

Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.

"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."

Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."

In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".

The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.

It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.

Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

articles.body: Wearing nothing but swimming trunks, goggles and a UN-branded cap, 56-year-old ocean campaigner Lewis Pugh entered the waters off Oman’s Musandam Peninsula, where he found himself swimming within sight of burning ships and towering plumes of smoke. The following day, he witnessed another vessel engulfed in flames as he continued his swim through the strategic waterway. A United Nations Patron of the Oceans, Pugh warned that pollution from damaged tankers could devastate coral reefs, mangroves and coastal ecosystems for decades. Yet sightings of dolphins, turtles and ospreys reminded him of the extraordinary wildlife at risk. Having previously swum in the Arctic, Antarctic and Red Sea to raise awareness of ocean conservation, he delivered a stark appeal: “We’ve got to stop the war. We’ve got to open the strait, and we’ve got to clean up this mess.”

articles.title: Nuova notte di attacchi in Ucraina, morti e feriti. Missile russo anche su Kiev
articles.summary: Nella capitale udita una potente esplosione, in fiamme edifici residenziali
articles.preview: Due persone, una donna e un bambino di sette anni, sono morte dopo un attacco russo avvenuto nella serata di venerdì, con missili balistici, nel centro di Kryvyi Rih. Quarantadue persone sono rimaste feritei. Lo hanno reso noto, scrive l'Ukrainska Pravda, il capo dell'amministrazione di Dnipropetrovsk, Oleksandr Ganzha, e Mykola Lukashuk, presidente del Consiglio regionale di Dnipropetrovsk.
articles.body:
Due persone, una donna e un bambino di sette anni, sono morte dopo un attacco russo avvenuto nella serata di venerdì, con missili balistici, nel centro di Kryvyi Rih. Quarantadue persone sono rimaste feritei.

Lo hanno reso noto, scrive l'Ukrainska Pravda, il capo dell'amministrazione di Dnipropetrovsk, Oleksandr Ganzha, e Mykola Lukashuk, presidente del Consiglio regionale di Dnipropetrovsk.

Su Telegram ill capo del Consiglio di Difesa di Kryvyi Rih, Oleksandr Vilkul, secondo quanto riportato da Ukrinform, ha riferito che "alle 23:00 si contavano già 42 feriti, di cui quattro bambini. Una ragazza di 20 anni e un bambino di 7 anni sono deceduti", ha scritto. Secondo Vilkul, 27 persone versano in gravi condizioni. I medici stanno fornendo a loro e a tutti i feriti tutta l'assistenza necessaria. Secondo i dati preliminari, 23 edifici residenziali, un ospedale e alcune strutture commerciali hanno subito danni.

Allerta aerea anche nella capitale. "Un'allerta aerea è stata dichiarata in nottata a Kiev per la minaccia di un attacco aereo con droni. In città si sono udite delle esplosioni". Lo rende noto l'aeronautica militare ucraina che ha anche "segnalato un drone a reazione diretto verso Kiev", riporta l'Ukrainska Pravda

Nel quartiere Podilskyi di Kiev, a seguito di un attacco russo, alcuni edifici residenziali privati hanno preso fuoco. Lo afferma l'amministrazione militare di Kiev su Telegram, riportata da Ukrinform. I russi avevano attaccato Kiev con un missile e una potente esplosione era stata udita nella capitale.

Il bilancio

Nella notte, la Russia ha attaccato l'Ucraina con tre missili balistici e 148 droni d'attacco, di cui 87 a reazione. Lo riporta Rbc-Ucraina citando l'Aeronautica militare ucraina. Secondo i dati preliminari, le difese aeree sono riuscite ad abbattere o neutralizzare 117 droni (di cui 67 a reazione), mentre i missili hanno superato le difese ucraine. Sono stati registrati attacchi aerei russi in 19 località, nonché la caduta di frammenti in 9 località. Questa mattina si sono verificate interruzioni nella fornitura idrica in cinque distretti di Kiev. Lo riporta RBC-Ucraina, riferendo che l'interruzione riguarda i quartieri di Holosiivskyi, Svyatoshynskyi, Solomyanskyi, Shevchenkivskyi e Podilskyi della capitale.

Mosca: 'Abbattuti 275 droni ucraini sulle regioni russe durante la notte'

Le forze russe hanno sferrato, nel corso della notte, attacchi contro infrastrutture energetiche e imbarcazioni utilizzate a supporto delle operazioni dell'esercito ucraino. Lo ha reso noto il Ministero della Difesa russo, scrive la Tass. "La scorsa notte, le Forze armate russe hanno condotto attacchi, mediante velivoli a pilotaggio remoto, contro strutture energetiche e imbarcazioni coinvolte nel sostegno alle operazioni dell'esercito ucraino", ha dichiarato il Ministero in un comunicato.

La Tass, su Telegram, fa sapere che un cargo civile è stato colpito mentre era in transito marittimo nelle vicinanze di Odessa, trasportando merci a doppio uso destinate a rifornire le forze armate ucraine. Le forze di difesa aerea russe hanno intercettato e distrutto 275 droni ucraini sulle regioni russe nel corso della notte. Lo ha reso noto il ministero della Difesa russo citato dall'agenzia Tass. "Durante la notte scorsa i sistemi di difesa aerea in stato di allerta hanno intercettato e distrutto 275 droni ucraini ad ala fissa sopra le regioni di Belgorod, Brjansk, Voronež, Kaluga, Kursk, Leningrado, Novgorod, Orël, Pskov, Rostov e Smolensk, la Repubblica di Crimea e le acque del Mar Nero", si legge nella nota del ministero.

articles.title: Around 700,000 displaced by volatile conflict in southern Ethiopia
articles.summary: NGO Islamic Relief says fighting between ethnic groups competing for land and wealth has seen widespread destruction of homes and disruption of services.
articles.preview: Ethiopia British NGO Islamic Relief says fighting sparked by a dispute over who controls the southern town of Moyale on Ethiopia’s border with Kenya has seen around 700,000 people displaced from their homes. It said on Thursday that clashes between members of the Oromo and Ethiopian Somali communities began in late October. articles.body:
Ethiopia

British NGO Islamic Relief says fighting sparked by a dispute over who controls the southern town of Moyale on Ethiopia’s border with Kenya has seen around 700,000 people displaced from their homes.

It said on Thursday that clashes between members of the Oromo and Ethiopian Somali communities began in late October.

Fighting involving heavy weaponry has now reportedly spread up to 300 kilometres from the town along the Kenya, Somalia, Ethiopian border.

"This is a volatile conflict driven by two ethnic groups competing for land and wealth in the borders of Ethiopia," said Kedir Musema Hameza, the head of Islamic Relief's Ethiopia programme.

The NGO said there has been widespread destruction of homes, businesses, and petrol stations, as well as disruption of essential services, including health, water, and sanitation.

It said access to the locations has been challenging and warns of a deepening humanitarian crisis.

Approximately 50,000 people have fled into Kenya placing additional pressure on local services and host communities.

The government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who hails from the Oromia region, has not commented on the violence.

The borders between the country's regions, set by the 1995 constitution, have been a frequent source of conflict in Ethiopia which currently faces multiple internal conflicts.

Just weeks ago, fighting erupted in Tigray, hundreds of kilometres to the north, when rebels and government forces clashed.

There have also been long-running insurgencies in the most populous regions of Amhara and Oromia that have displaced hundreds of thousands.

articles.preview: Despite dodging tears in the tarmac, people are confident in city’s infrastructure – and will not worry about what has not happened yet Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.
articles.body:
Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.

Buses are now the only motor transport allowed across the normally busy multi-lane crossing, though on their way into the city centre they have to skirt the tears in the tarmac, using the only functioning lane to get by.

“So what if there’s a hole? The bridge hasn’t collapsed. You need to know a bit about bridge construction,” says Mykola, 65, at the wheel of a half -full afternoon bus as it clatters on its way west.

Mykola operates a marshrutka, a single deck private bus, whose drivers are famed in Kyiv mythology for being able to multi-task: chatting, smoking and collecting fares, while driving as fast as possible to take passengers from rivals.

Passengers pay 25 hryvnia (42p) in cash and typically one passenger gets the unofficial job of taking money and handing back change on behalf of the driver. It turns out this has become the Guardian’s task, in order to conduct an interview.

“It would be very difficult to destroy the bridge. It would take a huge number of missiles, and if one or two hit it, it wouldn’t be the end of the world,” Mykola continues, with behind-the-wheel speculation that is so far accurate. By lunchtime the holes have been covered up, perhaps to avoid unsettling passengers eyeing the Dnipro River below.

Alongside its attacks on the capital’s electricity, heating and water systems, Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s bridges since early October, trying to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, home to about a third of its population.

Moscow struck the bridges twice again this week, first on Tuesday – overshadowed by Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch road bridge to Crimea. Then again during a noisy Thursday night, hours after Vladimir Putin promised there would be a “far more painful” response to the demolition of his pet project.

As of Friday, in an already traffic-snarled city, Kyiv’s other main road bridge, the Southern Bridge, was allowing motor traffic only from east to west. The new Podilskyi Bridge, damaged early on Friday, was similarly restricted, and the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, told people to avoid car travel after a night in which six were killed.

The Northern Bridge remains open for public transport – plus any cyclists, scooter riders and walkers willing to brave the damp late autumn weather and ignore missile and drone alerts. But below, earthworks have begun to prepare for a floating pontoon bridge, one of eight planned, in case of the worst.

Dmytro Bespalov, a transport planning expert with Kyiv’s National University of Construction and Architecture, said it was difficult to destroy a suspension bridge like the Northern. They have “a strong construction, with a lot of repairability”, meaning damage can usually be fixed. Though there are holes in the roadway, its supporting structures were so far unscathed, he added.

Russia is thought to have been aiming ballistic missiles at the supporting pylon, requiring a precise and difficult to execute attack, though that is what Ukraine did at the culmination of its complex attack on the Kerch road bridge, which was brought down after a Flamingo cruise missile struck its supporting arch.

Yet, Bespalov cautioned that Kyiv was strategically vulnerable if Russia targets the bridges with “dozens or hundreds” of missiles, because the city did not have enough bridges from before the war. “In 2021, Kyiv was in third place in Europe for congestion on the TomTom traffic index,” he said, behind Istanbul and Moscow.

Particular concern is reserved for the pontoon bridge alternative. They can bear less traffic: “It would take 20 pontoon bridges to have half the current capacity,” Bespalov said – and they are far more vulnerable to missile and drone attack. “I don’t think it would be possible to use pontoons during a red [missile] or yellow [drone] alarm” – not least because vehicles could end up in the water.

At the first busy bus stop on the eastern left bank, Nataliya, 40, and Iryna, 39, are happy to make the crossing over the Northern Bridge. They say they have long got used to the difficulties of war: “The main thing is to get through the first 24 hours at home after the initial discomfort, and then we’ll adapt,” said Nataliya, a customer service specialist.

Iryna added: “If we start to despair, that’s exactly what they want. A bridge can be built. The main thing is that when the attack comes, there are no civilians or military personnel around. It’s just concrete, that’s all. They’ll either repair it or come up with something new.”

It is a core attitude of Kyiv’s remaining residents, who are already contending with hours of electricity shortages and a lack of heating, with the full chill of winter yet to arrive. People want to deal with problems as they arise rather than worrying excessively about what may come – though it is not always easy amid the daily attacks, including a daytime raid on Thursday in which a drone exploded near the Dutch embassy.

Oleksandr, 42, a construction worker, was waiting to get across the bridge. “If the bridges are destroyed we’ll have to leave,” he conceded. If that happened, he and his wife would move to her parents’ house across the river. “I bought them a generator there; they have their own water well. We’d already dug the well during the war. They used to have gas heating, but we’ve converted it to wood-burning. We’re preparing,” he said.

articles.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Tehran still hoped diplomacy could end its war with the United States, while U.S. President Donald Trump said Iran wanted a deal but one that was not acceptable to him.

Araqchi told the state-owned Iran newspaper that messages continued to be exchanged between Iran and Washington through mediators, and that Tehran was seeking “an agreement that would ensure there was no further war.”

He also said Iran wanted guarantees that Washington was serious about negotiations before proceeding further, adding that Iran had discussed with mediators the form and nature of confidence-building measures.

The remarks came as diplomatic efforts continued to try to end a conflict that has destabilized the Middle East, disrupted shipping, driven up global energy prices and drawn in countries across the region.

The foreign minister said Iran’s red lines included keeping its highly enriched uranium in the country, though he said a “fair solution” was still possible.

Authorities have previously mentioned “feasible formulas” to resolve the dispute between Tehran and Washington over the matter, including diluting the highly enriched uranium stockpile under the supervision of the International Atomic Energy Agency.

The IAEA estimates that Iran had 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60% when Israel and the U.S. attacked Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025. How much of that has survived is unclear.

“I believe a fair solution can be reached on the issue of nuclear material, one that is based on our national interests while also meeting the country’s needs,” Araqchi said.

Trump, in a bews conference on Friday, said: “They want to make a deal, but they don’t want to make a deal that’s acceptable to me.”

The United States and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, prompting Tehran to strike Israel and Gulf states hosting U.S. military bases.

Qatari and Iranian officials met on Tuesday in talks aimed at “bridging perspectives and narrowing the gap between proposals presented on the ground,” a spokesperson for Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said.

articles.body:
THE HAGUE – The International Court of Justice’s landmark ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya will strengthen South Africa’s genocide case against Israel over the war in Gaza, legal experts said, establishing a precedent that genocidal intent can coexist with a military objective.

While the conflicts in Gaza and Myanmar are legally distinct, both cases before the World Court are based on allegations that states breached their obligations under the 1948 Genocide Convention.

On Thursday, the court found that Myanmar had violated the convention on multiple grounds stemming from mistreatment of the Muslim Rohingya minority by the armed forces.

articles.body:
Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.

In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.

Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.

At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.

“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.

He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.

“You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.

“We want them to build it here.”

With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built.

The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months.

China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China.

In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and said: “If they do, we’re going to fight.”

He added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.”

Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump said the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”.

“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president said. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran.

“I can’t speak to America,” he said, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.”

He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election.

“I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said.

Trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He said Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.”

And he said Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”

articles.title: Ukraine: Rescue teams search wreckage after deadly Russian strike on Kyiv
articles.summary: A Russian overnight attack on Kyiv, Ukraine, killed eight people on Friday 20 November 2026, according to Associated Press, leaving buildings and warehouses damaged across the capital. Firefighters battled blazes as emergency crews searched the wreckage and police collected evidence.
articles.preview: A Russian overnight attack on Kyiv, Ukraine, killed eight people on Friday 20 November 2026, according to Associated Press, leaving buildings and warehouses damaged across the capital. Firefighters battled blazes as emergency crews searched the wreckage and police collected evidence.
articles.body: Smoke billowed over Kyiv and flames tore through apartment blocks and offices after Russia unleashed more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles across Ukraine overnight, killing at least eight people, six of them in the capital, and injuring 15, according to Ukrainian authorities and emergency services. Alongside residential and commercial buildings, strikes hit hospitals, essential infrastructure and three bridges spanning the Dnipro River, leaving streets littered with shattered masonry, twisted metal and wrecked cars. Across the battered capital, firefighters battled blazes while rescue teams searched ruined structures for survivors, police combed the debris for forensic evidence and utility crews worked to restore vital services. Some fires had been brought under control, but responders continued working to extinguish remaining blazes, clear rubble and assess damage across the capital. The devastating barrage, coming just a day after an earlier wave of attacks damaged diplomatic premises in Kyiv, made good on Russian President Vladimir Putin’s warning of a "painful" retaliation for Ukraine’s strike on the Crimean Bridge earlier in the week.

articles.title: What we know about the latest Russian missile strikes on Ukraine

articles.body:
Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.

Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least nine dead.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied peninsula.

The latest Russian strikes coincided with a flurry of talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.

The BBC's Sarah Rainsford is in Kyiv after the night of strikes.

articles.title: Dl scuola, gli e-book spaccano la maggioranza. FI vota contro, poi l'emendamento passa in Senato
articles.summary: AGI - L'avvertimento era arrivato ieri: Forza Italia è contraria alla norma sugli e-book . Ma FdI ha tenuto il punto sull'emendamento che stabilisce per gli editori l'obbligo di vendere la versione digitale dei libri scolastici e universitari a un prezzo inferiore di almeno il 50% rispetto alle edizioni cartacee. E così la maggioranza al Senato si spacca, con gli azzurri che votano contro e Azione che si aggiunge ai voti favorevoli delle altre forze di centrodestra. L'emendamento passa in Aula L'emendamento, presentato al Decreto Scuola, che tra le altre norme introduce il tetto del 30% di alunni stranieri con insufficiente conoscenza dell'italiano nelle classi, viene prima bocciato in Commissione Bilancio, sempre con i voti contrari di Forza Italia. Poi, messo in votazione in Aula, passa per 8 voti di differenza (84 sì e 76 no), con il via libera di FdI, presenti in massa, Lega e Noi Moderati, a cui si aggiungono i voti dei calendiani. Contrarie tutte le altre forze di opposizione, che protestano in Aula con cartelli e slogan. Il decreto, alla fine, viene approvato con i sì di tutto il centrodestra (80 voti favorevoli e 46 contrari) e trasmesso alla Camera per il via libera definitivo. Il peso delle assenze e il passaggio alla Camera 'Pesano' le assenze tra le fila delle opposizioni, che avrebbero potuto ribaltare l'esito del voto. Intanto nella maggioranza si guarda già all'iter a Montecitorio. Il decreto va convertito in legge entro il 29 novembre. Fonti parlamentari azzurre spiegano che alla Camera FI potrebbe presentare un proprio emendamento sul tema degli e-book, mentre non viene escluso che il governo possa porre la questione di fiducia, visti anche i tempi ristretti per l'esame. Le opposizioni all'attacco Al di là di quanto accadrà nel passaggio a Montecitorio, le opposizioni ne approfittano per evidenziare le divisioni del centrodestra. "C'è un dato politico che non state considerando, Forza Italia ha dato la sfiducia al governo sulla scuola, su questo voto finisce la legislatura, se avete un briciolo di dignità riportate il Paese al voto", sentenzia il leader di Iv Matteo Renzi. "Il fatto politico della giornata è che mi sembra non ci sia più una maggioranza", incalza la segretaria del Pd Elly Schlein. Anche per M5s "la maggioranza è a pezzi. Hanno votato contro il loro stesso emendamento, è un nodo politico enorme. Non si sono dimessi dopo il referendum e dopo essersi spaccati sulla legge elettorale, non lo faranno nemmeno stavolta. Ma almeno prendano atto del fatto che sono in tilt e ritirino questa decreto", afferma il capogruppo Luca Pirondini. E Avs aggiunge: "C'è una spaccatura evidente dentro la maggioranza e diamo la parola agli elettori", chiosa Peppe De Cristofaro La replica di Forza Italia FI nega la spaccatura e minimizza la portata del voto: si tratta solo di un emendamento. "Non c'entra niente la tenuta della maggioranza, non c'entra niente il governo", tiene a puntualizzare il leader azzurro e vicepremier Antonio Tajani, che fa sapere di aver "avvisato in anticipo che avremmo votato contro, lo sapevano tutti. Lo sapeva la premier, erano tutti informati". E la capogruppo Stefania Craxi assicura: "Da Forza Italia non c'è stata nessuna sfida a nessuno e non c'è nessuna rottura della maggioranza". La posizione di Fratelli d'Italia Anche in FdI si preferisce non dare alcuna enfasi al voto odierno, rispedendo al mittente le accuse delle opposizioni. Non c'è nessuna crisi di governo, è la linea. Per di più, viene ricordato, il governo non è coinvolto, trattandosi di un emendamento parlamentare sul quale l'esecutivo stesso si è rimesso all'Aula. Certo, il no di FI non viene accolto con favore, ma non sorprende. Semmai, è sempre il ragionamento, è l'opposizione a uscirne male, non essendo riuscita a incassare una vittoria nonostante la non compattezza della maggioranza. Insomma, nessun casus belli e, soprattutto, nessuna conseguenza sulla tenuta di governo e maggioranza, spiegano fonti di FdI che, comunque, tengono a ribadire: la norma resta e verrà confermata alla Camera, nessun passo indietro . Centrosinistra e Italia Viva insistono sulla frattura Il centrosinistra non ha intenzione di mollare la presa e insiste sulla frattura che si è consumata al Senato. "Forza Italia ha votato con tutte le opposizioni dapprima in Commissione, affossando il provvedimento sugli e-book", dice il vicepresidente Iv Enrico Borghi, e "di fronte a questo risultato, Fratelli d'Italia ha sfidato il partito di Marina e Piersilvio Berlusconi, e ha ripresentato l'emendamento per l'Aula mandando il sottosegretario Fazzolari a fare da guardiano dei suoi e sfidando Forza Italia", afferma. La presenza di Fazzolari in Aula, sia nella giornata di ieri che oggi, viene rimarcata anche dal capogruppo Pd Francesco Boccia: "Sembra essere il dominus di questo decreto visto che pontifica attraverso i mezzi d'informazione e dà anche consigli alle opposizioni". Botta e risposta finale tra Schlein e Calenda A fine giornata arriva il botta e risposta tra Schlein e Calenda. La leader dem confessa: "Certo che mi preoccupa" che Azione abbia votato con la destra, "spero non sia una scelta definitiva". Replica il leader di Azione: "E Schlein vota con le case editrici contro un taglio del 50% del costo dei libri per i ragazzi. Spero sia un caso perché altrimenti ci troveremmo davanti a una progressista che guarda al progresso delle case editrici e non al fatto che i giovani italiani possano pagare meno i libri per studiare".

AGI - L'avvertimento era arrivato ieri: Forza Italia è contraria alla norma sugli e-book . Ma FdI ha tenuto il punto sull'emendamento che stabilisce per gli editori l'obbligo di vendere la versione digitale dei libri scolastici e universitari a un prezzo inferiore di almeno il 50% rispetto alle edizioni cartacee. E così la maggioranza al Senato si spacca, con gli azzurri che votano contro e Azione che si aggiunge ai voti favorevoli delle altre forze di centrodestra.

L'emendamento passa in Aula L'emendamento, presentato al Decreto Scuola, che tra le altre norme introduce il tetto del 30% di alunni stranieri con insufficiente conoscenza dell'italiano nelle classi, viene prima bocciato in Commissione Bilancio, sempre con i voti contrari di Forza Italia. Poi, messo in votazione in Aula, passa per 8 voti di differenza (84 sì e 76 no), con il via libera di FdI, presenti in massa, Lega e Noi Moderati, a cui si aggiungono i voti dei calendiani.

Contrarie tutte le altre forze di opposizione, che protestano in Aula con cartelli e slogan. Il decreto, alla fine, viene approvato con i sì di tutto il centrodestra (80 voti favorevoli e 46 contrari) e trasmesso alla Camera per il via libera definitivo. Il peso delle assenze e il passaggio alla Camera 'Pesano' le assenze tra le fila delle opposizioni, che avrebbero potuto ribaltare l'esito del voto.

Intanto nella maggioranza si guarda già all'iter a Montecitorio. Il decreto va convertito in legge entro il 29 novembre. Fonti parlamentari azzurre spiegano che alla Camera FI potrebbe presentare un proprio emendamento sul tema degli e-book, mentre non viene escluso che il governo possa porre la questione di fiducia, visti anche i tempi ristretti per l'esame. Le opposizioni all'attacco Al di là di quanto accadrà nel passaggio a Montecitorio, le opposizioni ne approfittano per evidenziare le divisioni del centrodestra.

"C'è un dato politico che non state considerando, Forza Italia ha dato la sfiducia al governo sulla scuola, su questo voto finisce la legislatura, se avete un briciolo di dignità riportate il Paese al voto", sentenzia il leader di Iv Matteo Renzi. "Il fatto politico della giornata è che mi sembra non ci sia più una maggioranza", incalza la segretaria del Pd Elly Schlein. Anche per M5s "la maggioranza è a pezzi.

Hanno votato contro il loro stesso emendamento, è un nodo politico enorme. Non si sono dimessi dopo il referendum e dopo essersi spaccati sulla legge elettorale, non lo faranno nemmeno stavolta. Ma almeno prendano atto del fatto che sono in tilt e ritirino questa decreto", afferma il capogruppo Luca Pirondini. E Avs aggiunge: "C'è una spaccatura evidente dentro la maggioranza e diamo la parola agli elettori", chiosa Peppe De Cristofaro La replica di Forza Italia FI nega la spaccatura e minimizza la portata del voto: si tratta solo di un emendamento.

"Non c'entra niente la tenuta della maggioranza, non c'entra niente il governo", tiene a puntualizzare il leader azzurro e vicepremier Antonio Tajani, che fa sapere di aver "avvisato in anticipo che avremmo votato contro, lo sapevano tutti. Lo sapeva la premier, erano tutti informati". E la capogruppo Stefania Craxi assicura: "Da Forza Italia non c'è stata nessuna sfida a nessuno e non c'è nessuna rottura della maggioranza".

La posizione di Fratelli d'Italia Anche in FdI si preferisce non dare alcuna enfasi al voto odierno, rispedendo al mittente le accuse delle opposizioni. Non c'è nessuna crisi di governo, è la linea. Per di più, viene ricordato, il governo non è coinvolto, trattandosi di un emendamento parlamentare sul quale l'esecutivo stesso si è rimesso all'Aula. Certo, il no di FI non viene accolto con favore, ma non sorprende.

Semmai, è sempre il ragionamento, è l'opposizione a uscirne male, non essendo riuscita a incassare una vittoria nonostante la non compattezza della maggioranza. Insomma, nessun casus belli e, soprattutto, nessuna conseguenza sulla tenuta di governo e maggioranza, spiegano fonti di FdI che, comunque, tengono a ribadire: la norma resta e verrà confermata alla Camera, nessun passo indietro . Centrosinistra e Italia Viva insistono sulla frattura Il centrosinistra non ha intenzione di mollare la presa e insiste sulla frattura che si è consumata al Senato.

"Forza Italia ha votato con tutte le opposizioni dapprima in Commissione, affossando il provvedimento sugli e-book", dice il vicepresidente Iv Enrico Borghi, e "di fronte a questo risultato, Fratelli d'Italia ha sfidato il partito di Marina e Piersilvio Berlusconi, e ha ripresentato l'emendamento per l'Aula mandando il sottosegretario Fazzolari a fare da guardiano dei suoi e sfidando Forza Italia", afferma.

La presenza di Fazzolari in Aula, sia nella giornata di ieri che oggi, viene rimarcata anche dal capogruppo Pd Francesco Boccia: "Sembra essere il dominus di questo decreto visto che pontifica attraverso i mezzi d'informazione e dà anche consigli alle opposizioni". Botta e risposta finale tra Schlein e Calenda A fine giornata arriva il botta e risposta tra Schlein e Calenda. La leader dem confessa: "Certo che mi preoccupa" che Azione abbia votato con la destra, "spero non sia una scelta definitiva".

Replica il leader di Azione: "E Schlein vota con le case editrici contro un taglio del 50% del costo dei libri per i ragazzi. Spero sia un caso perché altrimenti ci troveremmo davanti a una progressista che guarda al progresso delle case editrici e non al fatto che i giovani italiani possano pagare meno i libri per studiare".

articles.preview: Il ceo di Anthropic, Dario Amodei, che ieri mattina è atterrato a Brindisi, starebbe partecipando a un evento organizzato da una società italiana di consulenza e servizi informatici nel resort Borgo Egnazia, a Fasano. articles.body:
Il ceo di Anthropic, Dario Amodei, che ieri mattina è atterrato a Brindisi, starebbe partecipando a un evento organizzato da una società italiana di consulenza e servizi informatici nel resort Borgo Egnazia, a Fasano. L'azienda, a quanto si apprende, si occupa, tra l'altro, di intelligenza artificiale e analisi dei dati, cloud e infrastrutture digitali, e cybersecurity.

"Per noi - spiega all'ANSA il sindaco di Fasano, Francesco Zaccaria - essere diventati un punto di riferimento, ogni giorno, per gente che arriva da ogni parte del mondo, ci riempie chiaramente di orgoglio e soprattutto ripaga il lavoro svolto negli ultimi anni. La consacrazione del G7 ci ha permesso di mostrare al mondo la nostra parte migliore del nostro territorio".

Continuano intanto a circolare le ipotesi di un suo possibile investimento immobiliare. Nell'ultimo anno alcuni suoi stretti collaboratori avrebbero più volte visitato la Puglia per valutare l'acquisto di una lussuosa masseria. Mentre un'altra possibile operazione potrebbe riguardare l'acquisto, per il quale ci sarebbero trattative in corso, di un resort situato tra le province di Bari e Brindisi.

"Certo siamo tutti contenti che lui è qui, ma - sottolinea il sindaco di Brindisi Pino Marchionna - è in forma assolutamente privata. Ho avuto modo di parlare anche con altre autorità che non erano state informate in quanto lui è sceso come un privato cittadino, è arrivato con un volo diretto da New York, ha fatto i controlli di frontiera come qualunque cittadino normale e noi dobbiamo rispettare la privacy di questa persona". "Ci fa molto piacere che personaggi di tale caratura, all'indomani di una performance straordinaria sul piano borsistico - conclude - abbiano scelto la provincia di Brindisi, il nostro aeroporto, dopo momenti di grande stress".

The intrusion into the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), which federal, state and local law enforcement agencies use to share criminal justice information, was discovered in recent days, CNN reported . The FBI has called it a central law enforcement information system used by agencies across the country. The potential consequences extend beyond the theft of sensitive information. A former FBI official who led investigations into cybercriminal groups said that officers rely on the database to identify fugitives, check outstanding warrants and access information. “My concern isn’t simply whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on,” the former official told CNN. FBI director Kash Patel addressed the bureau's cybersecurity efforts on Fox News on Thursday, after officials had learned of the latest intrusion. Patel touted Operation Winter Shield , an initiative launched earlier this year to encourage companies to strengthen their digital defences and protect sensitive information. “Other administrations could have made these updates, but they didn’t,” he said. “We are staying ahead of the curve and making up for lost time.” The FBI launched Operation Winter Shield in February as a cybersecurity campaign aimed at helping private-sector organisations strengthen their information technology and operational technology systems. A week of outages The FBI incident has unfolded alongside a series of technology disruptions affecting major US institutions. On 13 November, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop after a technical problem disrupted its air traffic communications network, grounding flights for several hours . US air travel thrown into chaos as nationwide flights grounded over 'radar instability' ng to Reuters. The FAA said the problem began when its legacy telecommunications system became unstable after receiving an unusually high volume of data through its network. Days earlier, a global outage affecting Microsoft's services disrupted Outlook, Teams and its Copilot assistant, affecting organisations across several countries. The outage affected businesses, banks, hospitals, courts, airlines and government agencies. Downdetector received reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories. On 16 November, customers reported difficulties accessing online services at several major US banks, including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and US Bank. The following day, the National Security Agency's classified internal communications network, known as NSANet, also experienced an outage .
